```{python}
#| label: setup
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib as mpl
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
from statsmodels.nonparametric.smoothers_lowess import lowess
from scipy import stats
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

mpl.rcParams.update({
    "figure.dpi": 120, "axes.grid": True,
    "grid.alpha": 0.25, "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False,
    "font.size": 11, "axes.titlesize": 12,
})
WING = "#2c7fb8"   # blue
TAIL = "#756bb1"   # purple
TARS = "#31a354"   # green
MASS = "#d95f0e"   # orange

# trait registry — feather traits (wing, tail), skeletal (tarsus), soft tissue (mass)
ORDER = ["lnwing", "lntail", "lntar", "lnmass"]
COL = {"lnwing": WING, "lntail": TAIL, "lntar": TARS, "lnmass": MASS}
LAB = {"lnwing": "wing length", "lntail": "tail length",
       "lntar": "tarsus length", "lnmass": "body mass"}
SRC = {"lnwing": "cwl", "lntail": "ctail", "lntar": "ctar", "lnmass": "mass"}

def fmt(x, d=4): return f"{x:+.{d}f}"
```

## The puzzle, widened

The main analysis of this project found that **wing length declined** across 89
Atlantic Forest passerine species between 1990 and 2018 (Bayesian phylogenetic
multilevel model, standardized year effect **β = −0.73 mm** per SD-year,
95 % CI −1.09 to −0.37, excluding zero), while a parallel model for **log body
mass** found essentially **no trend** (β = −0.001 log-g per SD-year, 95 % CI
−0.008 to +0.006). If birds are getting structurally smaller, why does their mass
not shrink too?

This report explores that question descriptively across **four proxies of body
size**: two flight-feather traits — **wing length** and **tail length** — a
leg/skeletal trait, **tarsus length**, and the soft-tissue measure, **body
mass**. Tarsus is conceptually the cleanest index of structural size; mass the
crudest (it fluctuates with gut content, fat, hydration); the feather traits sit
in between and additionally carry molt/wear signals. Throughout, we also track
whether each bird was measured **live or as a museum specimen**, since
preservation can bias measurements and could confound a temporal trend (developed
in the descriptive section below and tested formally in @sec-status). The result
is richer than the original two-trait puzzle:

> The four proxies **do not move together**. Within species, wing length
> declines, tarsus length *increases*, and tail length and body mass show no net
> change — so the wing decline is not a coordinated whole-body shrinkage. But the
> *shape* of the trends matters: wing length and tail length (the two feather
> traits) both fall sharply in the most recently sampled years, a recent signal a
> single linear slope hides.

## Reproducing the analytical sample

We rebuild the exact analytical frame used by the project's models directly from
the raw ATLANTIC BIRD TRAITS csv (filters: `Year ≥ 1990`, adult, known sex,
Passeriformes, inside the 20-km Atlantic Forest buffer; then species with ≥ 30
records and a ≥ 5-year span). This reproduces the canonical sample of **15,332
records / 89 species** exactly. Wing, tail and tarsus each coalesce
right/left/unspecified measurements the way the project's wing variable is built.

```{python}
#| label: load
RAW = "../data/raw/ATLANTIC_BIRD_TRAITS_completed_2018_11_d05.csv"
b = pd.read_csv(RAW, low_memory=False)

mask = (
    (b.Year >= 1990) & (b.Age == "Adult") &
    (b.Sex.isin(["Male", "Female"])) &          # R's filter drops NA sex too
    (b.Order == "Passeriformes") &
    (b.AtlanticForests_20km_Buffer == "inside the 20 km polygon")
)
d = b[mask].copy()
d["cwl"]  = (d["Wing_length_right.mm."].combine_first(d["Wing_length_left.mm."])
             .combine_first(d["Wing_length.mm."]))
d["ctail"] = (d["Tail_length_right.mm."].combine_first(d["Tail_length_left.mm."])
              .combine_first(d["Tail_length.mm."]))
d["ctar"] = (d["Tarsus_length_right.mm."].combine_first(d["Tarsus_length_left.mm."])
             .combine_first(d["Tarsus_length.mm."]))
d["Binomial"] = d["Binomial"].str.replace(" ", "_")
d = d[d.groupby("Binomial")["Binomial"].transform("size") >= 30].copy()
d = d[d.groupby("Binomial")["Year"].transform(lambda x: x.max() - x.min()) >= 5].copy()

d["scaled_yr"]  = (d.Year - d.Year.mean()) / d.Year.std()
d["scaled_lat"] = ((-d.Latitude_decimal_degrees) - (-d.Latitude_decimal_degrees).mean()) \
                   / (-d.Latitude_decimal_degrees).std()
d["mass"] = d["Body_mass.g."]
for resp, src in SRC.items():
    d[resp] = np.log(d[src])
YR_SD = d.Year.std()

print(f"Records: {len(d):,}   Species: {d.Binomial.nunique()}   (expect 15,332 / 89)\n")
print("Trait coverage within the sample (and species with ≥30 records of the trait):")
for resp in ORDER:
    src = SRC[resp]; sub = d.dropna(subset=[src])
    n30 = (sub.groupby("Binomial").size() >= 30).sum()
    print(f"  {LAB[resp]:14s}: {sub[src].notna().sum():>6,} records, "
          f"{sub.Binomial.nunique():>2} species ({n30} with ≥30)")
print(f"\nYear SD (for per-SD ↔ per-year conversion): {YR_SD:.2f} years")
```

All four traits are well sampled (~10,000–14,000 records). Body mass is actually
the *best* sampled, so nothing here is limited by data volume.

## A first note on data quality (tarsus)

Tarsus length contains some physically impossible values — passerine tarsi run
roughly 10–35 mm, yet a handful exceed 50 mm (e.g. a 192 mm tarsus on a
*Herpsilochmus* antwren, ~18 mm in life). These are data-entry errors. We keep all
records in the main analysis for consistency with the project's pipeline (which
likewise keeps a 480 g mass outlier), but flag the issue here and show the tarsus
trend is **robust to removing implausible values** — it even strengthens. A
systematic, four-trait outlier analysis follows in @sec-outliers.

```{python}
#| label: tarsus-qc
def mixed_yr(df, resp):
    sub = df.dropna(subset=[resp]).copy()
    f = smf.mixedlm(f"{resp} ~ C(Sex) + scaled_yr + scaled_lat", sub,
                    groups=sub["Binomial"], re_formula="~scaled_yr").fit(method="lbfgs")
    b1, se = f.params["scaled_yr"], f.bse["scaled_yr"]
    return b1, se, f.pvalues["scaled_yr"], len(sub)

imp = d.ctar.notna() & ((d.ctar < 5) | (d.ctar > 40))
print(f"Implausible tarsus records (<5 or >40 mm): {imp.sum()} of {d.ctar.notna().sum()}")
for name, df in [("all records", d), ("plausible 5–40 mm only", d[~imp])]:
    b1, se, p, n = mixed_yr(df, "lntar")
    print(f"tarsus, {name:24s}: β_yr = {b1:+.4f} "
          f"[{b1-1.96*se:+.4f}, {b1+1.96*se:+.4f}], p = {p:.3f}, N = {n:,}")
```

## What the four traits look like

Each bird was measured either **live** (mist-netting) or as a **museum** specimen,
and we carry that distinction through from here. The colours below are fixed:
<span style="color:#3182bd"><b>live</b></span> and
<span style="color:#e6550d"><b>museum</b></span>.

```{python}
#| label: dist-counts
#| echo: false
LIVE_C, MUS_C = "#3182bd", "#e6550d"
ds = d[d.Status.isin(["live", "museum"])].copy()
print(f"Sample by measurement status: live {int((ds.Status=='live').sum()):,} | "
      f"museum {int((ds.Status=='museum').sum()):,} | unknown {int((~d.Status.isin(['live','museum'])).sum())}")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-dist
#| fig-cap: "Distributions on the modelled log scale, overlaid by measurement status (density-normalised so the two groups are comparable despite very different sample sizes). The live and museum distributions broadly overlap for every trait — at the whole-sample scale, between-species variation dwarfs any status effect."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(11, 6.5))
for a, resp in zip(ax.ravel(), ORDER):
    for st, c in [("live", LIVE_C), ("museum", MUS_C)]:
        x = ds.loc[ds.Status == st, resp].dropna()
        a.hist(x, bins=40, density=True, color=c, alpha=.5, label=st)
    a.set_title(f"log {LAB[resp]}"); a.set_xlabel(f"log({SRC[resp]})")
    a.set_ylabel("density"); a.legend()
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(d[[SRC[r] for r in ORDER]].describe().round(2).to_string())
```

At the whole-sample scale the live and museum curves sit almost on top of each
other, because between-species variation is enormous (and exactly why pooling
across species, next, is the wrong tool). But that overlap *hides* the status
effect: a 5 % shift in tail is invisible against a trait that varies several-fold
across species. To expose it we re-plot the same data as **within-species
deviations** (each record minus its species mean), which removes the
between-species spread:

```{python}
#| label: fig-dist-status
#| fig-cap: "Within-species deviations (% from each species' mean) by status. Once between-species spread is removed, the systematic museum bias is clear: museum tail length reads longer and museum body mass lighter, while wing is essentially unaffected. Dashed lines = group means. This is the same effect quantified in @sec-status."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(11, 6.5))
for a, resp in zip(ax.ravel(), ORDER):
    sub = ds.dropna(subset=[resp]).copy()
    sub["dev"] = (sub[resp] - sub.groupby("Binomial")[resp].transform("mean")) * 100
    for st, c in [("live", LIVE_C), ("museum", MUS_C)]:
        x = np.clip(sub.loc[sub.Status == st, "dev"], -25, 25)
        a.hist(x, bins=45, density=True, color=c, alpha=.5, label=st)
        a.axvline(sub.loc[sub.Status == st, "dev"].mean(), color=c, ls="--", lw=2)
    a.set_title(f"log {LAB[resp]}"); a.set_xlabel("within-species deviation (%)")
    a.set_ylabel("density"); a.legend()
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-status-desc
#| fig-cap: "Descriptive statistics by measurement status."
rows = []
for resp in ORDER:
    src = SRC[resp]
    for st in ["live", "museum"]:
        x = ds.loc[(ds.Status == st), src].dropna()
        dev = (ds.loc[ds.Status == st, resp] -
               ds.groupby("Binomial")[resp].transform("mean")).dropna()
        rows.append([LAB[resp], st, f"{len(x):,}", f"{x.mean():.2f}", f"{x.median():.2f}",
                     f"{x.std()/x.mean():.3f}", f"{dev.mean()*100:+.2f}%"])
pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["trait","status","n","mean","median","CV","mean within-spp dev"])
```

The descriptive table makes the point numerically: museum specimens read longer in
tail (and slightly in tarsus) and lighter in mass, with wing barely touched. Since
museum specimens are not evenly spread over time, we test whether this biases the
*trends* in @sec-status — it does not for wing, tarsus or mass, and only matters
for tail.

## The trap: pooling across species reverses the sign

A naïve approach regresses each trait on year across *all* records at once, with
the covariates the models use (sex, latitude).

```{python}
#| label: naive
rows = []
for resp in ORDER:
    sub = d.dropna(subset=[resp])
    f = smf.ols(f"{resp} ~ scaled_yr + C(Sex) + scaled_lat", data=sub).fit()
    b1 = f.params["scaled_yr"]; lo, hi = f.conf_int().loc["scaled_yr"]
    rows.append([f"log {LAB[resp]}", len(sub), fmt(b1), f"[{fmt(lo)}, {fmt(hi)}]"])
pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["trait", "N", "β (per SD-yr, log)", "95% CI"])
```

Several naïve pooled slopes come out **positive** — including wing length, which
we *know* declines within species. This is Simpson's paradox: the pooled slope
mixes genuine within-species change with shifts in *which* species were sampled
over time, and between-species variation is so large that composition dominates.
**The pooled trend is uninformative.** The right question is within-species, which
the random-slope structure of the project's models isolates — reproduced next.

## Within-species trends: the four traits diverge

### Per-species slopes

For each species we fit a within-species regression of the log trait on
standardized year — the model-free analogue of a random year slope.

```{python}
#| label: perspp
def per_species(resp):
    out = []
    for sp, g in d.dropna(subset=[resp]).groupby("Binomial"):
        if g.Year.nunique() < 3 or g[resp].nunique() < 2:
            continue
        out.append(smf.ols(f"{resp} ~ scaled_yr", data=g).fit().params["scaled_yr"])
    return np.array(out)

slopes = {r: per_species(r) for r in ORDER}
rows = []
for resp in ORDER:
    s = slopes[resp]; neg, pos = int((s < 0).sum()), int((s > 0).sum())
    sign_p = stats.binomtest(min(neg, pos), neg + pos).pvalue
    rows.append([f"log {LAB[resp]}", len(s), fmt(np.median(s)), fmt(s.mean()),
                 f"{pos}/{neg+pos}", f"{sign_p:.3f}"])
pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["trait", "species", "median slope", "mean slope",
                            "increased", "sign-test p"])
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-slopes
#| fig-cap: "Within-species year slopes (log scale, per SD-year), one panel per trait. Dashed = median, solid black = zero. Wing slopes sit left of zero (most decline); tarsus right of zero (most increase); tail and body mass straddle zero."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(11, 7), sharex=True)
bins = np.linspace(-0.06, 0.06, 31)
for a, resp in zip(ax.ravel(), ORDER):
    s = np.clip(slopes[resp], bins[0], bins[-1])
    a.hist(s, bins=bins, color=COL[resp], alpha=.8, edgecolor="white")
    a.axvline(np.median(slopes[resp]), color=COL[resp], ls="--", lw=2,
              label=f"median {np.median(slopes[resp]):+.4f}")
    a.axvline(0, color="black", lw=1)
    a.set_title(f"log {LAB[resp]}", loc="left"); a.set_ylabel("species"); a.legend(loc="upper right")
for a in ax[-1]: a.set_xlabel("within-species slope of log(trait) on standardized year")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The four traits point different ways. Wing declines in most species (sign-test
p = 0.001); tarsus *increases* in most (p = 0.001); tail and body mass are near
coin-flips (p ≈ 0.4 and 0.2).

### A like-for-like mixed model

Matching the project's models without the phylogeny: a random-intercept /
random-year-slope mixed model per trait
(`trait ~ sex + scaled_yr + scaled_lat + (1 + scaled_yr | species)`).

```{python}
#| label: mixed
rows = []
for resp in ORDER:
    b1, se, p, n = mixed_yr(d, resp)
    rows.append([f"log {LAB[resp]}", fmt(b1), f"[{fmt(b1-1.96*se)}, {fmt(b1+1.96*se)}]",
                 f"{p:.3f}", f"{n:,}"])
pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["trait", "β year (per SD-yr, log)", "95% CI", "p", "N"])
```

Without any phylogenetic machinery this reproduces and extends the headline:
**wing length declines** (CI excludes zero, p < 0.001), **tarsus length increases**
(p ≈ 0.03; p = 0.001 once impossible values are dropped), and **tail length and
body mass show no net trend** (CIs span zero). Three of the four proxies fail to
show the wing decline; one moves the opposite way. The flat mass result is not a
quirk of the Bayesian model, and the wing decline is clearly *not* a uniform
skeletal shrinkage.

## Putting all four traits on a common scale

The original "−0.73 vs −0.001" headline mixes units (mm vs log-grams). Expressing
every within-species slope as a **percentage change per decade** (a log slope `β`
≈ a fractional change `expm1(β)`) makes them directly comparable.

```{python}
#| label: fig-commonscale
#| fig-cap: "Within-species change per decade (%) with 95% CI (mixed models). Wing length declines ~2%/decade (CI below zero); tarsus rises ~2%/decade (CI above zero); tail length and body mass sit on zero. The proxies diverge in direction and in statistical support."
res = {}
for resp in ORDER:
    b1, se, p, n = mixed_yr(d, resp); f = 10 / YR_SD
    res[resp] = (np.expm1(b1*f)*100, np.expm1((b1-1.96*se)*f)*100, np.expm1((b1+1.96*se)*f)*100)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3.3))
order = ["lnmass", "lntail", "lnwing", "lntar"]
for i, resp in enumerate(order):
    est, lo, hi = res[resp]
    ax.errorbar(est, i, xerr=[[est-lo],[hi-est]], fmt="o", color=COL[resp], ms=11, capsize=5, lw=2)
    ax.text(est, i+0.22, f"{est:+.2f}%/decade", ha="center", color=COL[resp], fontsize=10)
ax.axvline(0, color="black", lw=1)
ax.set_yticks(range(len(order))); ax.set_yticklabels([LAB[r] for r in order])
ax.set_ylim(-0.6, len(order)-0.3); ax.set_xlabel("within-species change per decade (%)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
for resp in ORDER:
    e, l, h = res[resp]; print(f"  {LAB[resp]:14s}: {e:+.2f}%/dec  [{l:+.2f}, {h:+.2f}]")
```

On a common footing, wing and tarsus change at *similar magnitudes in opposite
directions* (~±2 %/decade), while tail length and body mass barely move. Body mass
being flat is therefore corroborated by *two* other proxies, not explained away.

## The shape of the trends over time (non-linearity within 1990–2018) {#sec-time}

A single linear slope can hide acceleration, plateaus or reversals. We probe the
*shape* of each trend two ways, both on **within-species deviations** (each record
minus its species mean, so between-species composition is removed): (1) mean
deviation in five time bins, and (2) a LOWESS smoother across years. We do **not**
extend before 1990 — only ~1,250 records exist earlier, with essentially no body
mass (one record before 1970) and likely different collection methods, so it would
add high-leverage noise rather than signal.

```{python}
#| label: fig-nonlinear
#| fig-cap: "Within-species deviation (%) of each trait over time: dots = mean ± SE in five period bins, line = LOWESS smoother. Wing length (blue) and tail length (purple) — the two feather traits — both fall steeply in the most recently sampled years; tarsus (green) rises steadily; body mass (orange) hugs zero throughout. Note sampling is sparse in the 1990s and densest after 2005."
BINS = [(1990,1999),(2000,2004),(2005,2009),(2010,2014),(2015,2018)]
centers = [np.mean(x) for x in BINS]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 7.5), sharex=True)
for a, resp in zip(ax.ravel(), ORDER):
    sub = d.dropna(subset=[resp]).copy()
    sub["dev"] = (sub[resp] - sub.groupby("Binomial")[resp].transform("mean")) * 100
    lo = lowess(sub["dev"], sub["Year"], frac=0.6, return_sorted=True)
    a.plot(lo[:,0], lo[:,1], color=COL[resp], lw=2.5, zorder=3)
    for (lo_y, hi_y), c in zip(BINS, centers):
        v = sub[(sub.Year>=lo_y)&(sub.Year<=hi_y)]["dev"]
        a.errorbar(c, v.mean(), yerr=v.sem(), fmt="o", color=COL[resp], ms=7,
                   capsize=4, mec="white", zorder=4)
    a.axhline(0, color="black", lw=1)
    a.set_title(f"log {LAB[resp]}", loc="left"); a.set_ylabel("within-species deviation (%)")
for a in ax[-1]: a.set_xlabel("year")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: quad
rows = []
for resp in ORDER:
    sub = d.dropna(subset=[resp]).copy()
    sub["dev"] = sub[resp] - sub.groupby("Binomial")[resp].transform("mean")
    sub["yr2"] = sub["scaled_yr"]**2
    f = smf.ols("dev ~ scaled_yr + yr2", data=sub).fit()
    rows.append([LAB[resp], fmt(f.params["scaled_yr"]), f"{f.pvalues['scaled_yr']:.3f}",
                 fmt(f.params["yr2"], 5), f"{f.pvalues['yr2']:.3f}"])
pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["trait", "linear β", "linear p", "quadratic β", "quadratic p"])
```

The temporal shape is itself informative:

- **Wing length** declines *non-linearly and recently*: it sits slightly above the
  species mean through the 2000s and then drops sharply in 2015–2018 (~−1.7 %); the
  quadratic term is strongly negative (p < 0.001). The decline is concentrated in
  the most recent years rather than spread evenly across 28 years.
- **Tail length**, though *net* flat, shows the **same recent fall** (~−1.7 % in
  2015–2018; significant negative quadratic) — so the two feather traits move
  together in the recent window even though only wing has a significant linear
  trend. This hints at a shared recent flight-feather signal (true size change, or
  molt/wear/measurement shifts) that the linear model misses.
- **Tarsus length** rises steadily and essentially *linearly* (quadratic n.s.,
  p ≈ 0.49) — a monotone increase across the whole window.
- **Body mass** stays on zero in every bin and shows no linear *or* quadratic term
  (both p > 0.3). There is no hidden non-linear mass change at any timescale.

### Controlling for measurement status

Because the museum:live mix changes over time (@sec-status), we re-draw each
trajectory **separately by status**, centering within species *and* status so that
each curve shows only the temporal *shape* within its own measurement type (the
constant museum offset is removed).

```{python}
#| label: fig-nonlinear-status
#| fig-cap: "Within-(species×status) deviation (%) over time, split by measurement status — live (blue) and museum (orange); line = LOWESS, dots = period means ± SE (shown where n ≥ 15). The live series (the bulk of the data) reproduces every shape: wing's recent fall, tarsus's steady rise, tail's hump-then-recent-fall, and mass's flatness. Museum records are sparse — especially after 2010 (≈37–150 records in 2015–2018) — and erratic, but show no systematic opposing pattern. The recent feather-trait drop is clearly a live-data phenomenon, not a preservation artifact."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 7.5), sharex=True)
for a, resp in zip(ax.ravel(), ORDER):
    sub = ds.dropna(subset=[resp]).copy()
    sub["dev"] = (sub[resp] - sub.groupby(["Binomial", "Status"])[resp].transform("mean")) * 100
    for st, c in [("live", LIVE_C), ("museum", MUS_C)]:
        g = sub[sub.Status == st]
        if len(g) > 30:
            lo = lowess(g["dev"], g["Year"], frac=0.6, return_sorted=True)
            a.plot(lo[:, 0], lo[:, 1], color=c, lw=2.5, label=st, zorder=3)
        for lo_y, hi_y in BINS:
            v = g[(g.Year >= lo_y) & (g.Year <= hi_y)]["dev"]
            if len(v) >= 15:
                a.errorbar(np.mean([lo_y, hi_y]), v.mean(), yerr=v.sem(), fmt="o",
                           color=c, ms=6, capsize=3, mec="white", zorder=4)
    a.axhline(0, color="black", lw=1)
    a.set_title(f"log {LAB[resp]}", loc="left")
    a.set_ylabel("within-(species×status) dev (%)"); a.legend(fontsize=9)
for a in ax[-1]: a.set_xlabel("year")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: nonlinear-status-tbl
rows = []
for resp in ORDER:
    sub = ds.dropna(subset=[resp]).copy()
    sub["dev"] = (sub[resp] - sub.groupby(["Binomial", "Status"])[resp].transform("mean")) * 100
    for st in ["live", "museum"]:
        g = sub[sub.Status == st]
        cells = []
        for lo_y, hi_y in BINS:
            v = g[(g.Year >= lo_y) & (g.Year <= hi_y)]["dev"]
            cells.append(f"{v.mean():+.2f}% (n{len(v)})" if len(v) else "—")
        rows.append([LAB[resp], st] + cells)
pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["trait", "status", "1990–99", "2000–04", "2005–09", "2010–14", "2015–18"])
```

Read trait by trait, controlled by status:

- **Wing** — the **live** series carries the whole story: gently above the species
  mean through the 2000s, then a sharp drop in 2015–2018 (−1.7 %). Museum wing is
  flat/noisy on a small sample and does not reproduce (or oppose) the decline.
- **Tarsus** — the steady increase is clear in the **live** series (−1.6 % → +2.1 %);
  museum tarsus is erratic but ends positive too.
- **Tail** — the hump-then-recent-fall holds in the **live** series; museum tail
  swings wildly (a function of ~200–440 records spread thinly across years) and is
  best disregarded for shape.
- **Body mass** — flat in **both** status groups across every period; the only
  notable museum point is a 2015–2018 dip on just ~150 records, well within noise.

So the temporal shapes are **properties of the live data**, not of the changing
museum fraction. Museum specimens are too few — and too unevenly spread across
years — to define a trajectory, but where they appear they do not contradict the
live series.

So "deeper time changes" exist — but as **non-linearity within 1990–2018**, not
something recoverable by extending the record backward. The most striking is that
the wing (and tail) decline is a recent phenomenon, robust to measurement status,
which the project's linear slope understates.

## Signal-to-noise: how blunt is each instrument?

Part of why body mass is uninformative is that it is a much noisier index of size.
We quantify this with the within-species coefficient of variation (CV) per trait
(each on the species with ≥ 30 records of it).

```{python}
#| label: fig-cv
#| fig-cap: "Within-species coefficient of variation by trait (one point per species; black bar = median). Wing length is the cleanest (~0.06), tail and tarsus intermediate, body mass the noisiest (~0.14). High individual-level noise lowers power to resolve a small temporal shift — but tarsus, though noisier than wing, still resolves a clear (opposite) trend, so noise alone cannot explain the flat traits."
cvrows = []
for resp in ORDER:
    src = SRC[resp]; sub = d.dropna(subset=[src])
    cvs = sub.groupby("Binomial").apply(lambda g: g[src].std()/g[src].mean()
                                        if len(g) >= 30 else np.nan).dropna()
    for v in cvs: cvrows.append((LAB[resp], v))
cv = pd.DataFrame(cvrows, columns=["trait", "cv"])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 4.3))
for j, resp in enumerate(ORDER):
    vals = cv.loc[cv.trait == LAB[resp], "cv"].values
    jit = np.random.RandomState(j).normal(0, .05, len(vals))
    ax.scatter(np.full(len(vals), j)+jit, vals, color=COL[resp], alpha=.65, edgecolor="white")
    ax.scatter(j, np.median(vals), color="black", marker="_", s=700, lw=2.5, zorder=3)
ax.set_xticks(range(len(ORDER))); ax.set_xticklabels([LAB[r] for r in ORDER])
ax.set_ylabel("within-species CV"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print("Median within-species CV:")
for resp in ORDER:
    print(f"  {LAB[resp]:14s}: {cv.loc[cv.trait==LAB[resp],'cv'].median():.3f}")
```

Body mass carries ~2.4× the within-species noise of wing length; tail and tarsus
are intermediate. Noise is part of why mass is uninformative — but **not** the
whole story: tarsus is noisier than wing yet still resolves a clear opposite
trend, proving the flat traits cannot be blamed on noise alone.

## Does the mass–wing relationship shift? (allometry / condition)

If wing shrinks while mass holds, are birds heavier *for their wing*? We regress
log mass on log wing within species and test whether the residual
("mass-for-wing" condition index) trends over time.

```{python}
#| label: allometry
bw = d.dropna(subset=["lnmass", "lnwing"]).copy()
allo = smf.mixedlm("lnmass ~ lnwing", bw, groups=bw["Binomial"],
                   re_formula="~lnwing").fit(method="lbfgs")
bw["cond"] = bw["lnmass"] - (allo.params["Intercept"] + allo.params["lnwing"]*bw["lnwing"])
ct = smf.mixedlm("cond ~ scaled_yr", bw, groups=bw["Binomial"],
                 re_formula="~scaled_yr").fit(method="lbfgs")
b1, se = ct.params["scaled_yr"], ct.bse["scaled_yr"]
print(f"Within-species allometric slope (log mass ~ log wing): {allo.params['lnwing']:.2f}")
print(f"Mass-for-wing (condition) trend: {b1:+.4f} [{b1-1.96*se:+.4f}, {b1+1.96*se:+.4f}] "
      f"per SD-yr, p = {ct.pvalues['scaled_yr']:.3f}")
```

The within-species allometric slope is shallow (~0.4): wing explains only a modest
fraction of individual mass variation, so the two are partly decoupled. The
mass-for-wing residual shows **no significant temporal trend** (p ≈ 0.20). The
size proxies are loosely yoked — a change in one need not appear in the others.

## Sanity check: early-vs-late quartile comparison

The model-free comparison the project reports for each trait — mean log trait in
the early (≤ 2006) vs late (≥ 2013) period, per species.

```{python}
#| label: fig-quartile
#| fig-cap: "Per-species change in mean log trait, late (≥2013) minus early (≤2006). Wing: most species decrease. Tarsus: most increase. Tail and body mass: roughly even."
pq = d[(d.Year <= 2006) | (d.Year >= 2013)].copy()
pq["period"] = np.where(pq.Year <= 2006, "early", "late")
def quartile(resp):
    t = (pq.dropna(subset=[resp]).groupby(["Binomial","period"])[resp].mean().unstack().dropna())
    return (t["late"] - t["early"]).sort_values()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(14, 3.2))
for a, resp in zip(ax, ORDER):
    dd = quartile(resp)
    a.bar(range(len(dd)), dd.values, color=[COL[resp] if v>0 else "#9e9e9e" for v in dd.values])
    a.axhline(0, color="black", lw=1); a.set_xticks([])
    a.set_title(f"{LAB[resp]}\n{(dd>0).sum()}↑ / {(dd<0).sum()}↓ (n={len(dd)})", loc="left", fontsize=10)
    a.set_xlabel("species, sorted")
ax[0].set_ylabel("Δ mean log trait (late − early)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The quartile picture matches the slopes: wing down, tarsus up, tail and mass split.

## Within-species outliers and their influence on the trends {#sec-outliers}

How far do the results depend on a few aberrant records *within species*? We
detect within-species outliers with a robust rule, cross-check them against an
independent signal (left vs right measurements), and re-estimate every trend with
the outliers removed or tamed.

### Detecting within-species outliers (robust MAD rule)

For each species and trait we compute a **robust z-score** on the log scale,
`z = (log x − median) / (1.4826 · MAD)`. Median/MAD are themselves resistant to
outliers, so a single aberrant value cannot define the threshold. We flag
`|z| > 3.5`.

```{python}
#| label: mad-detect
def mad_z(df, resp):
    g = df.groupby("Binomial")[resp]
    med = g.transform("median")
    mad = g.transform(lambda x: (x - x.median()).abs().median()) * 1.4826
    return (df[resp] - med) / mad.replace(0, np.nan)

rows = []
for resp in ORDER:
    z = mad_z(d, resp); n = d[resp].notna().sum()
    rows.append([LAB[resp], f"{n:,}"] +
                [f"{(z.abs()>t).sum()} ({(z.abs()>t).mean()*100:.2f}%)" for t in (3.5, 4, 5)])
pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["trait", "N", "|z|>3.5", "|z|>4", "|z|>5"])
```

Outliers are uncommon in every trait (most frequent in tarsus, ~3.4 %; least in
wing, ~1.7 %). The most extreme records are unambiguous data errors — decimal
shifts, dropped digits, unit confusion:

```{python}
#| label: worst-records
worst = []
for resp in ORDER:
    src = SRC[resp]; z = mad_z(d, resp)
    tmp = d.assign(absz=z.abs()).nlargest(3, "absz")
    for _, r in tmp.iterrows():
        med = d.loc[d.Binomial == r.Binomial, src].median()
        worst.append([LAB[resp], r.Binomial.replace("_"," "), f"{r[src]:.1f}",
                      f"{med:.1f}", f"{r.absz:.0f}", int(r.Year)])
pd.DataFrame(worst, columns=["trait","species","value","species median","MAD-z","year"])
```

A 192 mm tarsus where the species sits at 19 mm, a 6.8 g thrush where it sits at
69 g (a dropped digit) — clerical, not biological. Do they move the trends?

### Cross-check: left vs right measurements

Where both sides were measured, the two should agree to within a couple of
percent; large asymmetries flag error independently of the MAD rule. (Tail and
mass have too few paired-side records to assess.)

```{python}
#| label: fig-lr
#| fig-cap: "Relative left–right difference |L−R|/mean for records measured on both sides. Tarsus is highly self-consistent; wing shows a heavier tail of large asymmetries (impossible for paired wings), an independent sign of clerical error in some wing records. Dashed = 5%."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.8))
for a, (L, R, nm, c) in zip(ax, [
        ("Wing_length_left.mm.","Wing_length_right.mm.","wing", WING),
        ("Tarsus_length_left.mm.","Tarsus_length_right.mm.","tarsus", TARS)]):
    sub = d.dropna(subset=[L, R])
    rel = (sub[R]-sub[L]).abs()/((sub[R]+sub[L])/2)*100
    a.hist(np.clip(rel, 0, 20), bins=40, color=c, alpha=.85)
    a.axvline(5, color="black", ls="--", lw=1)
    a.set_title(f"{nm}  (N={len(sub)} measured both sides)")
    a.set_xlabel("|left − right| / mean (%)"); a.set_ylabel("records")
    print(f"{nm}: median {rel.median():.2f}% | >5%: {(rel>5).sum()} | >10%: {(rel>10).sum()}")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Tarsus is internally very consistent (median 1.1 %, one record above 10 %) — its
errors are isolated gross values, not pervasive sloppiness. Wing, despite being
*least* outlier-prone overall, carries more large left–right discrepancies: no
trait is error-free.

### Do the outliers change the trends?

We re-estimate each trait's year trend under four treatments: **all** records,
**dropping** `|z|>4` and `|z|>3.5`, and **winsorizing** each species to its
1st–99th percentile. To avoid the random-slope mixed model's numerical instability
on trimmed subsets (its SEs inflate erratically when a few records are removed), we
use a transparent, convergence-free estimator: the **mean of within-species
slopes, with a species-bootstrap 95 % CI**.

```{python}
#| label: fig-sensitivity
#| fig-cap: "Year trend (% per decade, 95% species-bootstrap CI) for each trait under four outlier treatments. Body mass and tail length stay on/near zero; tarsus stays positive and strengthens as errors are removed; wing stays negative and excludes zero throughout, attenuating from ~−1.9% to ~−1.1%/decade. No trend is created, reversed or destroyed by outlier handling."
def spp_slopes(df, resp):
    out = {}
    for sp, g in df.dropna(subset=[resp]).groupby("Binomial"):
        if g.Year.nunique() < 3 or g[resp].nunique() < 2: continue
        out[sp] = smf.ols(f"{resp} ~ scaled_yr", data=g).fit().params["scaled_yr"]
    return pd.Series(out)
def boot_ci(s, n=2000, seed=1):
    rng = np.random.RandomState(seed); v = s.values
    return np.percentile([rng.choice(v, len(v), replace=True).mean() for _ in range(n)], [2.5, 97.5])
def winsor(df, resp, lo=.01, hi=.99):
    df = df.copy()
    df[resp] = df.groupby("Binomial")[resp].transform(lambda x: x.clip(x.quantile(lo), x.quantile(hi)))
    return df

pd_ = lambda x: np.expm1(x * 10 / YR_SD) * 100
rules = ["all", "drop |z|>4", "drop |z|>3.5", "winsor 1–99%"]
sens = {}
for resp in ORDER:
    z = mad_z(d, resp)
    dsets = [d, d[~(z.abs()>4)], d[~(z.abs()>3.5)], winsor(d, resp)]
    sens[resp] = [tuple(pd_(np.r_[s.mean(), boot_ci(s)]))
                  for s in (spp_slopes(df, resp) for df in dsets)]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 4.7))
off = {"lnwing": .24, "lntail": .08, "lntar": -.08, "lnmass": -.24}
for resp in ORDER:
    for i, (est, lo, hi) in enumerate(sens[resp]):
        ax.errorbar(est, i+off[resp], xerr=[[est-lo],[hi-est]], fmt="o", color=COL[resp],
                    ms=7, capsize=4, lw=1.7, label=LAB[resp] if i == 0 else None)
ax.axvline(0, color="black", lw=1)
ax.set_yticks(range(len(rules))); ax.set_yticklabels(rules)
ax.set_xlabel("year trend (% per decade, 95% bootstrap CI)")
ax.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=9); ax.set_ylim(-0.6, len(rules)-0.4)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print("Year trend (%/decade, species-bootstrap CI) by trait × rule:")
for resp in ORDER:
    print(f"  {LAB[resp]}:")
    for rule, (e, l, h) in zip(rules, sens[resp]):
        print(f"     {rule:14s}: {e:+.2f}% [{l:+.2f}, {h:+.2f}]")
```

The verdict is clean and trait-specific:

- **Body mass** and **tail length** sit on/near zero under every treatment — no
  trend created or concealed by outliers.
- **Tarsus length** stays positive and *strengthens* as errors are removed
  (~+2.2 % → ~+2.9 %/decade) — the opposite of outlier-driven.
- **Wing length** stays negative with CI excluding zero under all four rules,
  attenuating modestly (~−1.9 % → ~−1.1 %/decade). Some *magnitude* rode on extreme
  records; **direction and significance do not**. (The mixed model loses
  significance for wing at one trimming threshold, but that is its SE inflating on
  the trimmed subset, not a reversal — the bootstrap above keeps wing firmly
  negative, which is why we prefer it here.)

Intra-species outliers **do not drive any conclusion**. If anything, cleaning the
data sharpens the picture: tarsus up, wing down, tail and mass flat.

## Does museum vs live measurement confound the trends? {#sec-status}

The dataset's `Status` field records whether each bird was measured **live**
(mist-netting; 13,102 records here) or as a **museum** specimen (skin; 2,202
records). Museum skins can differ systematically from live birds — soft tissue
desiccates, feathers can shrink or shift — so if the museum:live mix changed over
time, a measurement artifact could masquerade as a temporal trend. We test this
directly.

### Museum specimens are concentrated in the early years

```{python}
#| label: status-composition
ds = d[d.Status.isin(["live", "museum"])].copy()
PER = [(1990,1999),(2000,2004),(2005,2009),(2010,2014),(2015,2018)]
print("Museum fraction of records by period:")
for lo, hi in PER:
    s = ds[(ds.Year >= lo) & (ds.Year <= hi)]
    print(f"  {lo}–{hi}: {100*(s.Status=='museum').mean():5.1f}% museum   (n = {len(s):,})")
print(f"\n  corr(museum indicator, year) = {np.corrcoef((ds.Status=='museum').astype(int), ds.Year)[0,1]:+.3f}")
```

This is exactly the setup for a confound: the museum share falls from ~41 % in the
1990s to ~6 % in 2015–2018. If museum specimens measure differently, that
composition shift alone could induce an apparent trend.

### Status shifts the measurements — strongly for tail and mass

We estimate the within-species museum-vs-live difference for each trait
(`trait ~ status + sex + latitude`, species random intercept).

```{python}
#| label: status-effect
rows = []
for resp in ORDER:
    sub = ds.dropna(subset=[resp]).copy()
    f = smf.mixedlm(f"{resp} ~ C(Status) + C(Sex) + scaled_lat", sub,
                    groups=sub["Binomial"]).fit(method="lbfgs")
    c = f.params["C(Status)[T.museum]"]; se = f.bse["C(Status)[T.museum]"]
    rows.append([LAB[resp], f"{np.expm1(c)*100:+.2f}%",
                 f"[{np.expm1(c-1.96*se)*100:+.2f}, {np.expm1(c+1.96*se)*100:+.2f}]",
                 f"{f.pvalues['C(Status)[T.museum]']:.3f}", int((sub.Status=='museum').sum())])
pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["trait", "museum vs live", "95% CI", "p", "n museum"])
```

Status genuinely affects the measurements: museum **tail length** reads ~5 % longer
and museum **body mass** ~1.8 % lighter (both p < 0.001), museum tarsus ~1 % longer
(p = 0.02), while **wing length is essentially unaffected** (+0.35 %, n.s.). Because
museum specimens dominate the early years, these biases could in principle distort
the temporal trends — so we re-estimate every trend four ways.

### The trends are robust to status — with one caveat (tail)

```{python}
#| label: fig-status
#| fig-cap: "Year trend (% per decade, 95% CI) for each trait under four status treatments: all records, adding Status as a covariate, live-only, and museum-only. Wing's decline and tarsus's increase are robust (and strengthen once status is accounted for); body mass stays flat throughout. Tail length is the exception — flat-to-negative on live records but positive on the (early, sparse) museum records — so tail trends are entangled with status."
def yreff(df, resp, extra=""):
    sub = df.dropna(subset=[resp]).copy()
    f = smf.mixedlm(f"{resp} ~ C(Sex)+scaled_yr+scaled_lat{extra}", sub,
                    groups=sub["Binomial"], re_formula="~scaled_yr").fit(method="lbfgs")
    b1, se = f.params["scaled_yr"], f.bse["scaled_yr"]; g = 10/YR_SD
    return (np.expm1(b1*g)*100, np.expm1((b1-1.96*se)*g)*100, np.expm1((b1+1.96*se)*g)*100,
            f.pvalues["scaled_yr"])

treat = ["all records", "+ Status covariate", "live-only", "museum-only"]
stat = {}
for resp in ORDER:
    stat[resp] = [yreff(ds, resp), yreff(ds, resp, "+C(Status)"),
                  yreff(ds[ds.Status=="live"], resp), yreff(ds[ds.Status=="museum"], resp)]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 4.9))
off = {"lnwing": .24, "lntail": .08, "lntar": -.08, "lnmass": -.24}
for resp in ORDER:
    for i, (est, lo, hi, p) in enumerate(stat[resp]):
        ax.errorbar(est, i+off[resp], xerr=[[est-lo],[hi-est]], fmt="o", color=COL[resp],
                    ms=7, capsize=4, lw=1.7, label=LAB[resp] if i == 0 else None)
ax.axvline(0, color="black", lw=1)
ax.set_yticks(range(len(treat))); ax.set_yticklabels(treat)
ax.set_xlabel("year trend (% per decade, 95% CI)")
ax.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=9); ax.set_ylim(-0.6, len(treat)-0.4)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

for resp in ORDER:
    print(f"{LAB[resp]}:")
    for t, (e, l, h, p) in zip(treat, stat[resp]):
        print(f"   {t:20s}: {e:+.2f}%/dec [{l:+.2f}, {h:+.2f}] p={p:.3f}")
```

The picture is reassuring for three of four traits:

- **Wing length** — decline robust everywhere: ~−1.9 %/decade at baseline, *stronger*
  once Status is controlled (−2.1 %) and on **live-only** records (−2.9 %, p < 0.001).
  Museum-only is the same direction (−1.1 %) but n.s. on its small, early sample.
  Since museum wing is barely different and museum records sit early, the confound
  if anything *suppresses* the decline slightly — the real signal is cleaner.
- **Tarsus length** — increase robust and *strengthens* once status is controlled
  (+2.7 %) and on live-only (+3.2 %). Museum tarsus reads larger and sits early, so
  the confound partly *masks* the increase; removing it sharpens the signal.
- **Body mass** — flat under every treatment (CI always spans zero). No status
  artifact creates or hides a mass trend.
- **Tail length** — the **caveat**. Tail is the most status-sensitive trait (+5 %
  museum bias) and its weak signal flips with treatment: flat-to-negative on
  live-only (−0.4 %/decade) but strongly positive on the early, sparse museum
  records (+4.6 %). Any tail trend is therefore entangled with status and should be
  read from the **live-only** estimate.

Finally, the recent (2015–2018) feather-trait drop from @sec-time survives
restricting to live birds — so it is not a museum artifact (the recent bins are
~94 % live anyway):

```{python}
#| label: status-recent
for resp, lab in [("lnwing","wing"), ("lntail","tail")]:
    for tag, sub0 in [("all ", ds), ("live", ds[ds.Status=="live"])]:
        sub = sub0.dropna(subset=[resp]).copy()
        sub["dev"] = (sub[resp] - sub.groupby("Binomial")[resp].transform("mean")) * 100
        v = sub[(sub.Year >= 2015) & (sub.Year <= 2018)]["dev"]
        print(f"  {lab} {tag}: 2015–2018 within-species deviation = {v.mean():+.2f}% (n {len(v)})")
```

**Bottom line:** museum-vs-live status is a real measurement effect and is
confounded with time (museum early), but it does **not** drive the core
inferences. Controlling for it leaves the wing decline and tarsus increase intact
(both *strengthen*), and body mass flat. The only trait whose trend is genuinely
status-dependent is tail length, whose net signal is weak and best taken from
live-only records.

## Conclusions

1. **The near-zero body-mass slope is real, not an artifact.** It is reproduced by
   a plain within-species mixed model with no phylogeny (β ≈ −0.002 log/SD-yr, CI
   through zero), rests on *more* data than the wing analysis, and is precisely
   estimated rather than merely uncertain.

2. **Four size proxies, four behaviours — they do not move together.** Within
   species: **wing length declines (~−2 %/decade), tarsus length increases
   (~+2 %/decade), and tail length and body mass show no net change.** Both
   directional results have sign-test p = 0.001, and tarsus strengthens when
   impossible values are removed.

3. **So this is not a uniform body-size reduction.** A whole-body Bergmann-style
   shrinkage would pull tarsus, tail and mass down with wing; instead tarsus rises
   and tail and mass are flat. The net change is **trait-specific to wing length**,
   cautioning against reading the wing decline as general "shrinking body size."

4. **But the temporal shape adds nuance (@sec-time).** The wing decline is
   *non-linear and recent* — concentrated in 2015–2018 (significant negative
   quadratic) — and **tail length, the other feather trait, falls in the same
   recent window** despite a flat net trend. At fine temporal resolution the two
   flight-feather traits align recently, which a single linear slope hides and
   which is worth following up (true recent size change vs molt/wear/measurement).

5. **"Deeper time" means non-linearity, not a longer record.** Extending before
   1990 is not advisable: only ~1,250 records exist earlier, with essentially no
   body mass (one record before 1970) and likely different methods. Sampling is
   itself back-loaded (the 1990s contribute < 1,000 records vs > 16,000 after
   2000), so the trends are anchored by recent decades — all the more reason to
   read them through the non-linear lens above.

6. **Body mass being flat is corroborated, not just unresolved.** Mass is the
   noisiest proxy (~2.4× the within-species CV of wing), lowering its power — but
   tarsus, though noisier than wing, resolves a clear opposite trend, so noise
   alone cannot explain the flat traits. Shallow mass–wing allometry (~0.4) and a
   non-trending condition index confirm the proxies are loosely coupled.

7. **The trends survive intra-species outlier handling (@sec-outliers).** Outliers
   are uncommon (1.7–3.4 %) and, where extreme, clearly clerical. Dropping or
   winsorizing them changes nothing essential: mass and tail stay flat, tarsus
   stays positive (strengthening), wing stays negative (attenuating).

8. **The trends survive the museum-vs-live confound (@sec-status).** Status is a
   real measurement effect (museum tail +5 %, mass −1.8 %, tarsus +1 %, wing
   negligible) and is confounded with time (museum specimens are concentrated in
   the early years), but it does not drive the inferences: controlling for status
   or restricting to live birds leaves the wing decline and tarsus increase intact
   (both *strengthen*) and mass flat. The recent feather-trait drop holds on
   live-only data. The one trait whose trend is genuinely status-dependent is
   **tail length** — weak and best read from live-only records.

9. **Methodological cautions.** Naïve pooling across species reverses the sign of
   the trends (Simpson's paradox). Tarsus carries the most measurement
   heterogeneity, so its *direction* is trustworthy but its magnitude approximate;
   tail/body-length-type feather and axial traits are noisier still. The
   random-slope mixed model can give unstable SEs on trimmed subsets, so robustness
   is best read from the species-bootstrap estimator. New trait results (tail,
   tarsus) and the recent-decline signal should be confirmed with the project's
   phylogenetic model before being reported alongside wing.

In short: bringing in tail length and tarsus shows the wing-length decline is
**specific**, not a coordinated body-size reduction — body mass does not decline
because there is no whole-body shrinkage to detect. Yet the two feather traits
fall together in the most recent years, a non-linear signal that deserves a closer
look.
